doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: Dummy faders and working with artists in big studios
summary: Hank rejects the trick of assigning a dead fader and describes how artists at Capitol and RCA were prepared by the time they reached the studio.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: You know I’ve had engineers tell me that on occasion they would assign a fader that did nothing, and if a producer or an ad person was in there and said can you give me a little more —
No? You didn’t have to do that?

Na, na, na. That’s bullshit. That’s like you’re killing the artist, you’re killing everybody. That’s baloney. You’ve got to make it work. You can’t hide anybody. Now I’m going to do this and then they won’t hear it? They’re going to hear it of course. You know —

The relationship in the bigger studios — Capitol, RCA, whatever — by the time you got an artist down there in the booth, I mean in the studio, they pretty well know what’s going on. They’ve heard the band, they’ve been there, done their work vocals. Sometimes you’ve got an artist that wants to do a finished vocal, they’re good enough to do it with the band out in the room, whether it be with a small rhythm session or a big band. The older artist working with a big band, Peggy Lee, whatever ensemble, but they’re used to working with a band. Then you get some of these artists that are not used to — they’re working with a small trio, now you start to dress them up with a rhythm section and studio players that are playing straight — you know you can’t have amateur hour now you know.
